title: Forward hum
purpose: Use an easy, forward hum to find light, efficient voicing, then carry it into vowels and words. The source presents this as part of lightening and brightening a voice.
instructions: Breathe in through your nose, then hum gently on a comfortable pitch. Notice any buzz at your lips and face.
Hum again, aiming the sound forward. A buzz at the lips usually comes with easy, efficient voicing; if you don't feel one, that's fine. What you're listening for is a brighter sound.
When that feels comfortable, keep smiling and move from the hum into a vowel: mmmee, mmmaa, mmmoo.
Then say short words that start with m, holding the m a little longer at first: meet, many, maybe, Mary, magic.

primary_cue.text: Aim the hum forward; your lips may tingle.

cues.text: Aim the hum forward; your lips may tingle.
Let a little air out through your nose just before you hum, like “hhhmmm”.
Imagine throwing your voice onto the ground in front of you.
Smile and start with a quiet hum, then slowly get a little louder, noticing whether your lips tingle.

practice_task.prompt_text: Hum forward, then say: mmmee, mmmaa, mmmoo — meet, many, maybe, Mary, magic.

check_questions.text: Listen back. Did the hum and the words after it sound brighter, and feel easy?

options.label: Easy, but I can't hear a change yet
It took effort or felt tight

check_questions.text: Where did you feel the buzz most? (Just a clue about easy voicing; any answer is fine.)

dose_guidance.text: This activity gives no repetition count. Take your time and don't move on too fast. The NHS Fife progression page suggests short, frequent practice in general.

expected_observations: A buzz at the lips and face, which usually comes with easy, efficient voicing.
Over time, a brighter sound in the words that follow the hum.
common_misunderstandings: Where you feel vibration isn't resonance itself: a chest buzz mostly comes with a lower or heavier voice, and any hum buzzes the face. Listen for brightness.
Pitch alone does not decide how a voice sounds.
Lighter does not mean quieter or whispery.
stop_conditions: Stop the activity if you feel pain or discomfort, or notice unintended voice changes such as hoarseness. The source says this may mean you are going too quickly.
Take time to look after your voice, and try again when it feels better.
If problems persist or keep coming back, seek advice from a voice professional such as a speech and language therapist.
adaptations: You can make up your own m-words.
You can stay on the hum and vowel steps for as long as you need.
limitations: Public NHS patient-advice material written for self-guided practice. Lilt cannot check your technique, and it does not replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt can't feel where your voice buzzes. Its resonance comparison works on held vowels only and is rough, so feedback here comes from what you report and from listening back.
